items.stem: What is a photon?
options: a particle of matter with charge e
the nucleus of a hydrogen atom
a quantum (discrete packet) of electromagnetic energy
items.answer: a quantum (discrete packet) of electromagnetic energy
items.markingKey: E = hf for each photon.

items.stem: Explain why photoelectric emission is instantaneous, even with very dim light.
items.answer: Each electron absorbs the energy of one photon in a single interaction; if hf exceeds the work function, emission happens at once. Energy does not need to build up gradually as wave theory predicts.
items.markingKey: one photon – one electron interaction [1]; no build-up time [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons does not depend on the intensity of the light.
items.answer: Each electron absorbs one photon of energy hf; intensity only changes the number of photons per second, not the energy of each, so Ek(max) = hf − Φ is unchanged.
items.markingKey: one photon per electron, energy hf [1]; intensity changes number of photons only [1] [2]

items.stem: A red laser pointer emits electromagnetic radiation of wavelength 6.50 × 10⁻⁷ m with a power of 0.0030 W. Determine the energy of one photon.
items.markingKey: E = hc/λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸/6.50 × 10⁻⁷ = 3.06 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A radio transmitter emits electromagnetic radiation of wavelength 3.0 m with a power of 1000 W. Calculate the energy of one photon, in J and in eV, and the number of photons emitted per second.

A green laser emits electromagnetic radiation of wavelength 5.32 × 10⁻⁷ m with a power of 0.020 W. (a) Calculate the number of photons emitted per second. (b) Calculate the momentum of one photon. (c) The beam is completely absorbed by a surface. Calculate the force on the surface.
items.markingKey: (a) E = hc/λ [1]; N = P/E = 5.35 × 10¹⁶ s⁻¹ [1] (b) p = h/λ = 1.25 × 10⁻²⁷ N s [1] (c) F = rate of change of momentum = Np [1]; = P/c = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N [1] [5]

items.stem: A laser emits light of wavelength 532 nm with an output power of 1.0 mW. (a) Calculate the number of photons emitted per second. (b) Explain why this light may not cause photoelectric emission from copper (work function 4.7 eV).
items.answer: (a) 2.67 × 10¹⁵ s⁻¹ (b) Photon energy 2.34 eV is less than the work function, so no electron can gain enough energy to escape.
items.markingKey: (a) N = P/E (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.67 × 10¹⁵ s⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) photon energy in eV [1]; less than Φ so no emission [1] [2]

items.stem: A laser emits light of wavelength 650 nm with an output power of 1.0 mW. (a) State what is meant by a photon. (b) Calculate the energy of a photon. (c) Explain why this light may not cause photoelectric emission from copper (work function 4.7 eV).
items.answer: (a) A discrete quantum (packet) of electromagnetic energy. (b) 3.06 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (c) Photon energy 1.91 eV is less than the work function, so no electron can gain enough energy to escape.
items.markingKey: (a) A discrete quantum (packet) of electromagnetic energy [1] (b) E = hc/λ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 3.06 × 10⁻¹⁹ J [1] [2] (c) photon energy in eV [1]; less than Φ so no emission [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the energy of a photon of frequency 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz?
Which expression gives the momentum of a photon of energy E?
items.answer: E/c
items.markingKey: p = E/c = h/λ.

items.stem: Explain how the photoelectric effect provides evidence for the particulate nature of electromagnetic radiation.
items.answer: The existence of a threshold frequency, the instant emission, and Ek(max) depending on frequency (not intensity) can only be explained if light arrives in discrete photons of energy hf, each absorbed by one electron.
items.markingKey: threshold frequency / instantaneous emission [1]; explained only by photons E = hf [1] [2]

items.stem: Show that the momentum of a photon is p = h/λ.
items.answer: E = hf = hc/λ and for a photon p = E/c, so p = (hc/λ)/c = h/λ.
items.markingKey: p = E/c [1]; substitute E = hc/λ [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Show that the momentum of a photon is p = h/λ. (b) Explain why the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons does not depend on the intensity of the light.
items.answer: (a) E = hf = hc/λ and for a photon p = E/c, so p = (hc/λ)/c = h/λ. (b) Each electron absorbs one photon of energy hf; intensity only changes the number of photons per second, not the energy of each, so Ek(max) = hf − Φ is unchanged.
items.markingKey: (a) p = E/c [1]; substitute E = hc/λ [1] [2] (b) one photon per electron, energy hf [1]; intensity changes number of photons only [1] [2]

items.stem: A radio transmitter emits electromagnetic radiation of wavelength 3.0 m with a power of 50 000 W. What is the energy of one photon?

items.markingKey: E = hc/(λe) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸/(4.00 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 3.11 eV. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Light of wavelength 700 nm is incident on a surface. Calculate the photon energy in electronvolts.
items.markingKey: E = hc/(λe) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸/(7.00 × 10⁻⁷ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹) = 1.78 eV. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: An ultraviolet lamp emits electromagnetic radiation of wavelength 2.54 × 10⁻⁷ m with a power of 5.0 W. (a) Calculate the number of photons emitted per second. (b) Calculate the momentum of one photon. (c) The beam is completely absorbed by a surface. Calculate the force on the surface.
items.markingKey: (a) E = hc/λ [1]; N = P/E = 6.39 × 10¹⁸ s⁻¹ [1] (b) p = h/λ = 2.61 × 10⁻²⁷ N s [1] (c) F = rate of change of momentum = Np [1]; = P/c = 1.67 × 10⁻⁸ N [1] [5]

items.stem: A laser emits light of wavelength 532 nm with an output power of 1.0 mW. (a) State what is meant by a photon. (b) Explain why this light may not cause photoelectric emission from copper (work function 4.7 eV).
items.answer: (a) A discrete quantum (packet) of electromagnetic energy. (b) Photon energy 2.34 eV is less than the work function, so no electron can gain enough energy to escape.
items.markingKey: (a) A discrete quantum (packet) of electromagnetic energy [1] (b) photon energy in eV [1]; less than Φ so no emission [1] [2]

items.stem: A laser emits light of wavelength 532 nm with an output power of 1.0 mW. (a) State what is meant by a photon. (b) Calculate the energy of a photon.
items.answer: (a) A discrete quantum (packet) of electromagnetic energy. (b) 3.74 × 10⁻¹⁹ J

items.stem: What is meant by the work function of a metal?
options: the energy needed to remove an electron from an atom of the metal in a gas
the kinetic energy of a free electron in the metal
the energy of the most energetic photoelectron
the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of the metal
items.answer: the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of the metal
items.markingKey: Φ = hf₀.

items.stem: Explain why there is a threshold frequency for photoelectric emission.
items.answer: Each electron absorbs one photon of energy hf; it can only escape if hf ≥ Φ. Below f₀ = Φ/h no single photon has enough energy, however many arrive.
items.markingKey: one photon per electron [1]; hf must be ≥ Φ, f₀ = Φ/h [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how a graph of Ek(max) against frequency can be used to find the Planck constant and the work function.
items.answer: Ek(max) = hf − Φ: a straight line with gradient h and intercept −Φ on the Ek axis (f₀ on the f axis, Φ = hf₀).
items.markingKey: gradient = h [1]; intercept gives −Φ or f₀ [1] [2]

items.stem: Light of wavelength 200 nm falls on a clean sodium surface. The work function of sodium is 2.3 eV. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.
items.markingKey: Ek = hc/λ − Φ = 9.95 × 10⁻¹⁹ − 3.68 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.27 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Light of wavelength 450 nm falls on a clean potassium surface. The work function of potassium is 2.3 eV. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons and their maximum speed.

Ultraviolet light of wavelength 350 nm is shone onto a calcium plate (work function 2.9 eV) connected to a sensitive ammeter circuit. (a) Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons. (b) State and explain the effect on the current of doubling the light intensity.
items.answer: (a) 1.04 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (b) Current doubles: twice as many photons per second release twice as many electrons.
items.markingKey: (a) hf − Φ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.04 × 10⁻¹⁹ J [1] [2] (b) current doubles [1]; twice as many photons per second [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is Einstein's photoelectric equation?
items.answer: hf = Φ + ½mv²(max)
items.markingKey: Photon energy = work function + maximum KE.

items.stem: Explain why graphs of Ek(max) against frequency for different metals are parallel lines.
items.answer: The gradient of each is h, the same universal constant; only the work function (intercept) differs between metals.
items.markingKey: gradient h for all [1]; different intercepts Φ [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the photoelectric current increases with intensity but Ek(max) does not.
items.answer: Greater intensity means more photons per second, so more electrons emitted per second (larger current); each photon still has energy hf, so Ek(max) is unchanged.
items.markingKey: more photons → more electrons [1]; same photon energy [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why the photoelectric current increases with intensity but Ek(max) does not. (b) Explain how a graph of Ek(max) against frequency can be used to find the Planck constant and the work function.
items.answer: (a) Greater intensity means more photons per second, so more electrons emitted per second (larger current); each photon still has energy hf, so Ek(max) is unchanged. (b) Ek(max) = hf − Φ: a straight line with gradient h and intercept −Φ on the Ek axis (f₀ on the f axis, Φ = hf₀).
items.markingKey: (a) more photons → more electrons [1]; same photon energy [1] [2] (b) gradient = h [1]; intercept gives −Φ or f₀ [1] [2]

items.stem: Ultraviolet light of wavelength 400 nm is shone onto a sodium plate (work function 2.3 eV) connected to a sensitive ammeter circuit. (a) Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons. (b) State and explain the effect on Ek(max) of doubling the intensity. (c) Explain why the electrons are emitted with a range of kinetic energies.
items.answer: (a) 1.29 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (b) No change: photon energy unchanged. (c) Electrons from below the surface lose energy in escaping; only surface electrons have Ek(max).
items.markingKey: (a) hf − Φ (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.29 × 10⁻¹⁹ J [1] [2] (b) No change: photon energy unchanged [1] (c) Electrons from below the surface lose energy in escaping; only surface electrons have Ek(max) [1]

items.answer: (a) 336 nm (b) Current doubles: twice as many photons per second release twice as many electrons. (c) No change: photon energy unchanged.

items.stem: Which experiment provides evidence that electrons have wave properties?
options: the deflection of electrons in a magnetic field
electron diffraction by a thin crystalline film
items.answer: electron diffraction by a thin crystalline film
items.markingKey: Rings are a diffraction pattern; λ = h/p.

items.stem: Explain what is meant by wave-particle duality.
items.answer: Both electromagnetic radiation and matter show wave properties in some experiments (diffraction, interference) and particle properties in others (photoelectric effect, collisions); neither model alone describes all behaviour.
items.markingKey: both waves and matter show both behaviours [1]; examples of each [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why electron diffraction is observed with graphite but not with a ruled diffraction grating for visible light.
items.answer: Electron wavelengths (~10⁻¹¹ m) are comparable with the spacing of atoms in graphite (~10⁻¹⁰ m); a ruled grating has spacing ~10⁻⁶ m, far too large to diffract the electrons noticeably.
items.markingKey: λ comparable to atomic spacing [1]; grating spacing too large [1] [2]

items.stem: Electrons are accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 50 V. Calculate the de Broglie wavelength.
items.markingKey: p = √(2meV) = 3.82 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹; λ = h/p = 1.74 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A proton moves at 5.0 × 10³ m s⁻¹. Calculate the momentum and the de Broglie wavelength of each particle.
items.markingKey: momentum method [1]; p = 8.35 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹ [1]; λ = h/p = 7.94 × 10⁻¹¹ m [1] [3]

items.stem: In an electron diffraction tube, electrons are accelerated through 4000 V and pass through a thin layer of graphite. Concentric rings are seen on a fluorescent screen. (a) Calculate the kinetic energy of an electron. (b) Calculate the de Broglie wavelength. (c) State and explain the effect on the rings of increasing the accelerating voltage.
items.answer: (a) 6.40 × 10⁻¹⁶ J (b) 1.94 × 10⁻¹¹ m (c) Rings get smaller: higher p gives smaller λ, so less diffraction.
items.markingKey: (a) Ek = eV: 6.40 × 10⁻¹⁶ J [1] (b) λ = h/p: 1.94 × 10⁻¹¹ m [1] (c) rings smaller [1]; larger p, smaller λ, less diffraction [1] [2]

items.stem: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of momentum p is …
items.answer: h/p
items.markingKey: λ = h/p.

items.stem: Explain why the diffraction rings get smaller when the accelerating voltage in an electron diffraction tube is increased.
items.answer: Higher V gives greater momentum (p = √(2meV)), so λ = h/p decreases; shorter wavelength is diffracted through smaller angles, giving smaller rings.
items.markingKey: greater p, smaller λ [1]; smaller diffraction angle [1] [2]

items.stem: Why do isolated atoms emit line spectra rather than continuous spectra?
options: the electrons have a continuous range of energies
the light is diffracted by the atoms
the atoms move with a range of speeds
the electrons can only occupy discrete energy levels
items.answer: the electrons can only occupy discrete energy levels
items.markingKey: Photon energy = difference between discrete levels.

items.stem: Explain how an emission line spectrum is produced by a hot gas.
items.answer: Electrons in the atoms are excited to higher energy levels; when they fall to lower levels each emits a photon of energy equal to the difference between the levels, hf = E₁ − E₂. Only certain differences exist, so only certain wavelengths (lines) appear.
items.markingKey: excitation then de-excitation [1]; photon energy = level difference, discrete [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why an absorption spectrum has dark lines at the same wavelengths as the emission lines of the same gas.
items.answer: Atoms absorb only photons whose energy equals a difference between their energy levels — the same differences that give the emission lines; these photons are removed from the beam and re-emitted in all directions, so the lines are dark.
items.markingKey: absorb photons of energy = level difference [1]; re-emitted in all directions so dark in beam direction [1] [2]

items.stem: Some energy levels of the hydrogen atom are −13.6 eV, −3.40 eV, −1.51 eV, −0.850 eV and −0.544 eV. An electron makes a transition from the −0.544 eV level to the −3.4 eV level. Determine the energy of the emitted photon.
items.markingKey: ΔE = −0.544 − (−3.4) = 2.86 eV. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Some energy levels of the hydrogen atom are −13.6 eV, −3.40 eV, −1.51 eV, −0.850 eV and −0.544 eV. An electron makes a transition from the −0.85 eV level to the −13.6 eV level. Calculate the wavelength of the photon emitted and state the region of the spectrum.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) How many different photon energies can be emitted by electrons moving between four energy levels? (b) A cool gas is placed between a white-light source and a spectrometer. What is observed?
items.answer: (a) 6 (b) dark lines on a continuous spectrum

items.stem: Explain why the spectrum of a gas provides evidence for discrete electron energy levels in atoms.
items.answer: Only specific wavelengths are emitted, so only specific photon energies; since hf = ΔE, only specific energy differences exist, which requires discrete levels.

items.answer: (a) Ek(max) = hf − Φ: a straight line with gradient h and intercept −Φ on the Ek axis (f₀ on the f axis, Φ = hf₀). (b) Greater intensity means more photons per second, so more electrons emitted per second (larger current); each photon still has energy hf, so Ek(max) is unchanged.
items.markingKey: (a) gradient = h [1]; intercept gives −Φ or f₀ [1] [2] (b) more photons → more electrons [1]; same photon energy [1] [2]

items.stem: Light of wavelength 300 nm falls on a clean sodium surface. The work function of sodium is 2.3 eV. Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain what is meant by wave-particle duality. (b) Explain why electron diffraction is observed with graphite but not with a ruled diffraction grating for visible light.
items.answer: (a) Both electromagnetic radiation and matter show wave properties in some experiments (diffraction, interference) and particle properties in others (photoelectric effect, collisions); neither model alone describes all behaviour. (b) Electron wavelengths (~10⁻¹¹ m) are comparable with the spacing of atoms in graphite (~10⁻¹⁰ m); a ruled grating has spacing ~10⁻⁶ m, far too large to diffract the electrons noticeably.
items.markingKey: (a) both waves and matter show both behaviours [1]; examples of each [1] [2] (b) λ comparable to atomic spacing [1]; grating spacing too large [1] [2]

items.stem: In an electron diffraction tube, electrons are accelerated through 3000 V and pass through a thin layer of graphite. Concentric rings are seen on a fluorescent screen. (a) Explain how the rings show that electrons behave as waves. (b) Calculate the momentum of an electron. (c) Calculate the de Broglie wavelength. (d) State and explain the effect on the rings of increasing the accelerating voltage.
items.answer: (a) Rings are a diffraction pattern, which is a wave property. (b) 2.96 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹ (c) 2.24 × 10⁻¹¹ m (d) Rings get smaller: higher p gives smaller λ, so less diffraction.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the spectrum of a gas provides evidence for discrete electron energy levels in atoms. (b) Explain how an emission line spectrum is produced by a hot gas.
items.answer: (a) Only specific wavelengths are emitted, so only specific photon energies; since hf = ΔE, only specific energy differences exist, which requires discrete levels. (b) Electrons in the atoms are excited to higher energy levels; when they fall to lower levels each emits a photon of energy equal to the difference between the levels, hf = E₁ − E₂. Only certain differences exist, so only certain wavelengths (lines) appear.
items.markingKey: (a) discrete wavelengths/energies [1]; implies discrete levels [1] [2] (b) excitation then de-excitation [1]; photon energy = level difference, discrete [1] [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why an absorption spectrum has dark lines at the same wavelengths as the emission lines of the same gas. (b) Explain how an emission line spectrum is produced by a hot gas.
items.answer: (a) Atoms absorb only photons whose energy equals a difference between their energy levels — the same differences that give the emission lines; these photons are removed from the beam and re-emitted in all directions, so the lines are dark. (b) Electrons in the atoms are excited to higher energy levels; when they fall to lower levels each emits a photon of energy equal to the difference between the levels, hf = E₁ − E₂. Only certain differences exist, so only certain wavelengths (lines) appear.
items.markingKey: (a) absorb photons of energy = level difference [1]; re-emitted in all directions so dark in beam direction [1] [2] (b) excitation then de-excitation [1]; photon energy = level difference, discrete [1] [2]

items.stem: Which observation of the photoelectric effect cannot be explained by a wave theory of light?
options: electrons are emitted from metal surfaces
the number of electrons emitted increases with intensity
the emitted electrons have a range of kinetic energies
no electrons are emitted below a threshold frequency, however intense the light
items.answer: no electrons are emitted below a threshold frequency, however intense the light
items.markingKey: Wave theory predicts emission at any frequency given enough intensity.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how the photoelectric effect provides evidence for the particulate nature of electromagnetic radiation. (b) Show that the momentum of a photon is p = h/λ.
items.answer: (a) The existence of a threshold frequency, the instant emission, and Ek(max) depending on frequency (not intensity) can only be explained if light arrives in discrete photons of energy hf, each absorbed by one electron. (b) E = hf = hc/λ and for a photon p = E/c, so p = (hc/λ)/c = h/λ.
items.markingKey: (a) threshold frequency / instantaneous emission [1]; explained only by photons E = hf [1] [2] (b) p = E/c [1]; substitute E = hc/λ [1] [2]
